title: Born of the Virgin (CCC 496–507)
hook: the Church professes Jesus was conceived by the Holy Spirit without a human father

segments.voice: Yesterday, Christ and Lord, two titles: anointed, and the name once kept for God. Your line was anointed. Today, how he was born.

A virgin in Nazareth, betrothed to a man named Joseph, has just been told she will have a son, that he will be great, and called the Son of the most High. Luke gives her one question, and it's a practical one. In the Douay-Rheims: "How shall this be done, because I know not man?" She isn't asking for a sign. She's asking how. And the angel's answer is the center of today: "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the most High shall overshadow thee." The Apostles' Creed folds that whole scene into a few words: born of the Virgin Mary.
screen: `A VIRGIN IN NAZARETH.` → `HOW SHALL THIS BE DONE?` → `THE HOLY GHOST SHALL COME UPON THEE.`

segments.voice: The Church confesses, the Catechism says, that Jesus was conceived solely by the power of the Holy Spirit in the womb of the Virgin Mary, with no human father. Luke tells it from Mary's side; Matthew from Joseph's. In Matthew, Joseph finds Mary with child and, being a just man, plans to send her away quietly. Then an angel in a dream tells him that what is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost, and he takes her home as his wife. The Catechism is honest that this isn't an easy teaching. People have objected; some have called it a legend. Its reply is not a proof: the Gospels present it as God's own work, beyond human understanding, whose meaning opens up only to faith. What does it mean, in Catholic teaching? First, the beginning is God's: Jesus has only God as his Father. Second, something new is starting: the Catechism calls Jesus the new Adam, the start of a new creation. Third, it's a sign for everyone else, a new birth by the Spirit, which Catholics connect with baptism. Day seventy-nine was the Immaculate Conception; this is a different teaching. The virginal conception is about how Jesus was conceived. The Immaculate Conception is about Mary herself, kept free from original sin from the first moment of her own life. And Mary's last line in Luke's scene is the one the Angelus repeats: "Behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it done to me according to thy word."
screen: `CONCEIVED BY THE HOLY SPIRIT ALONE.` · `LUKE FROM MARY'S SIDE, MATTHEW JOSEPH'S.` · `GOD'S WORK, OPEN TO FAITH.` · `NOT THE IMMACULATE CONCEPTION.` · then, large: `BE IT DONE TO ME ACCORDING TO THY WORD.`

segments.voice: The Angelus, an old Catholic prayer by tradition said when a church bell rings, walks through this very scene: the angel's message, Mary's answer, and the Word made flesh, with a Hail Mary between. If you pray and know it, pray it now, slowly. If you don't, stay with Mary's answer instead, be it done to me according to thy word, and notice how it feels to say yes to something you can't fully see.
Virginal conception. Jesus conceived by the Holy Spirit, with no human father; not the Immaculate Conception. Today's word.
Your line: by the holy spirit. A practical question, and then a yes. Day one thousand seventy-four.

howItsDone: Catholics profess the virginal conception in the Creed at Mass, and some pray the Angelus, a short prayer on the Annunciation said traditionally at morning, noon and evening.

chat.says: Is the Immaculate Conception about Jesus being born of a virgin?
options: No, that's the virginal conception. The Immaculate Conception is about Mary, kept free from original sin.
Yes, both names mean the same thing: Jesus conceived by the Spirit, with no human father.
No, it's about Joseph, chosen as a just man to raise Jesus without being his father.
chat.meaning: The virginal conception: Jesus conceived by the Holy Spirit, with no human father. The Immaculate Conception is a different teaching, about Mary kept free from original sin.

CCC paraphrased: conceived solely by the Holy Spirit (496), God's work beyond understanding (497), objections and 'accessible only to faith' (498), only God as Father (503), new Adam (504), sign of new birth (505). Immaculate Conception distinction from CCC 490–491 (outside the day's range; added to prevent a common confusion).
Practice describes the Angelus (three versicles with a Hail Mary after each; morning, noon and evening) without quoting it. Confirm the description.
Feast claim cut under the claims rule.
Original: παρθένος (Luke 1:27 has the accusative παρθένον). Keeper may prefer null.
Carry is lowercase 'by the holy spirit' as in the index; the voice says Holy Ghost only inside Douay-Rheims quotations.

Editor: 'young woman' became Luke's 'virgin, betrothed'; the Creed line is attributed to the Apostles' Creed (the Nicene wording at Mass differs); 'never been an easy teaching' softened; cut the uncited feast claim and the Angelus counts (three verses, three times a day).
Audit: cut the unsourced superlative that the Church keeps Mary's answer 'closest'; it is now tied to the Angelus, which the practice describes. Luke 1:34, 35, 38 Challoner wording checked.
